result: I concluded that the terminal FeCl3 group of the oxo-bridged [Cl3Fe–O–FeCl3] anion has rotational disorder, and I submitted a model that includes it. In the original model, the strongest difference peaks (about 0.9–1.5 e/Å³) sat 0.7–0.9 Å from Cl1, Cl2 and Cl3. Each of these peaks was about 2.2–2.4 Å from Fe2, which is what you'd expect for a second, rotated set of Fe–Cl bonds. I added a minor set of chlorines (Cl1B, Cl2B, Cl3B in PART 2, refined isotropically) that shares Fe2, with occupancies tied to a free variable. I restrained the Fe–Cl and Cl···Cl distances to be similar (SADI). The minor set refined to about 11%. R1 fell from 0.080 to 0.075, wR2 from 0.240 to 0.227 and GooF from 1.06 to 1.00, and the Fe–Cl distances (2.12–2.25 Å) are chemically sensible. Some of the residual peaks still sit on the other side of the chlorines (largest 1.5 e/Å³ near Cl3), so a third, very minor orientation may exist; I didn't model it. The benzyl ring (C17–C22) has large displacement parameters, but the peaks around it are weak (≤0.9 e/Å³), so I left it ordered along with the rest of the structure.
